repo_notes.content: This repository provides the openblink/mrubyc-esp32 ESP Component Registry package. vendor/mrubyc/ contains the unmodified mruby/c release3.4.1 sources. Kconfig and CMakeLists.txt configure the VM and compile wrapper sources for GPTimer compatibility and opt-in fatal diagnostics.

Version contract: component 3.4.1 bundles mruby/c release3.4.1, and Ruby sources must be compiled with mruby 3.4.0's mrbc (RITE0300); mruby 4.0.0 bytecode is rejected. A Registry version suffix such as 3.4.1~1 denotes a packaging revision, not a different VM.
README.md is the only user-facing document; there is no docs/ directory. Issues, pull requests, and code comments are written in English by repository policy.
tools/, test_app/, .github/, and .devin/ are development-only and excluded from the Registry archive by idf_component.yml. DeepWiki configuration stays in the repository.

pages.title: What does this component package?
pages.purpose: Overview of the component: which mruby/c sources it bundles, how the ESP-IDF build wiring exposes the VM and its ESP32 HAL to applications, and the version contract between component, mruby/c, mrbc, and RITE bytecode.

page_notes.content: vendor/mrubyc/ holds unmodified mruby/c release3.4.1 sources: src/ contains the VM and hal/esp32/ the upstream port's GPTimer-based scheduler timing and console output. CMakeLists.txt registers those directories directly as the component's SRC_DIRS.

gptimer_compat.c rejects CONFIG_GPTIMER_ISR_CACHE_SAFE with the hardware timer because its callback is not in IRAM. fatal_hooks.c implements opt-in diagnostics through mruby/c's upstream hooks without patching the VM.
Compile scripts with mruby 3.4.0's mrbc (RITE0300); mruby 4.0.0 emits a different bytecode format that release3.4.1 rejects. The component version tracks the mruby/c release.

pages.title: How do I compile and run a Ruby script?
pages.purpose: End-to-end flow from a .rb source to a running task: mrbc -B/--remove-lv header generation or EMBED_FILES .mrb embedding, the mrbc_init pool contract, mrbc_create_task, mrbc_run, and the single-task and lifetime rules.

page_notes.content: The README's app_main pattern: a static 8-aligned pool is passed to mrbc_init, the bytecode array to mrbc_create_task, then mrbc_run drives the scheduler. All examples and test_app follow this shape.

`mrbc --remove-lv -Bhello_bytecode -o main/hello_bytecode.h hello.rb` generates a const uint8_t array for #include. The alternative is `mrbc --remove-lv -o main/hello.mrb hello.rb`, which the main component embeds through EMBED_FILES "hello.mrb" (a component-relative path) and accesses via the asm symbol _binary_hello_mrb_start.

README constraints: keep the pool and backing bytecode alive for the scheduler's lifetime, invoke the VM from a single application task (not concurrently from other FreeRTOS tasks), and only load trusted bytecode.

pages.title: Which Kconfig options control the VM?
pages.purpose: The complete CONFIG_MRUBYC_* option map: what each Kconfig symbol does, its default, how CMake exports it as a compile definition, and the constraints between options (float, tick period versus FreeRTOS Hz, cache-safe GPTimer, NDEBUG propagation).

page_notes.content: Kconfig defines MAX_VM_COUNT=5, MAX_REGS_SIZE=110, MAX_SYMBOLS_COUNT=255, a single/double float choice (MRBC_USE_FLOAT=1/2), USE_MATH, USE_STRING_UTF8, USE_UNICODE_CASE (depends on UTF8), INT64, SUPPORT_OP_EXT on by default, ALLOC_LIBC, NO_TIMER, SCHEDULER_EXIT on, a 1/2/4/10 ms tick choice constrained by FREERTOS_HZ, TIMESLICE_TICK_COUNT=1, DEBUG, and CONVERT_CRLF.

CMakeLists.txt exports settings that affect public structures or APIs, including backtrace and task name capacity, profiling, and legacy value macros. KV table sizing, symbol search, Ruby stdio, register logging, and fatal hooks are private. Do not override component macros from consumer source files.

New runtime options retain the upstream defaults: tree search for dynamic symbols; 8 backtrace entries and 15 bytes per task name; key-value capacity starts at 2 and grows by 5. Profiling, register logging, and hiding stdio or legacy value macros are opt-in. NO_STDIO removes p, print, puts and printf but keeps sprintf.

MRBC_USE_FLOAT=0 is deliberately not offered: upstream release3.4.1 does not compile with it because some code still accesses floating-point fields. Only single and double precision are valid choices.
Disabling MRUBYC_DEBUG adds PUBLIC NDEBUG, which also disables C assertions in components that depend on this one, because public structures must agree on debug fields.

pages.title: How is the vendored mruby/c source kept unmodified?
pages.purpose: How vendor/mrubyc tracks upstream release3.4.1 without source edits: what is vendored, what is excluded, how intentional warnings are demoted per-target, and how the example bytecode headers are regenerated.

page_notes.content: idf_component.yml's files.exclude drops upstream-only files (vendor/mrubyc/src/Makefile, hal_selector.mk, UnicodeData.txt) along with .github/, .devin/, tools/, test_app/, build outputs, and sdkconfig artifacts from the Registry package.

Rather than patch upstream, CMakeLists.txt demotes two intentional diagnostics to warnings only for the vendored target: -Wno-error=implicit-fallthrough (load.c) and -Wno-error=unterminated-string-initialization when the compiler recognizes that warning.
Example bytecode headers are committed so firmware builds need no Ruby toolchain; from a checkout they are regenerated with tools/generate_bytecode.sh using mruby 3.4.0's mrbc.

pages.title: What do the examples demonstrate?
pages.purpose: The three examples under examples/: hello (init and run), vm_tasks (two scheduled tasks sharing a pool), and m5stack (a C/C++ binding that calls M5Unified from Ruby), including what is and is not hardware-verified.

page_notes.content: hello runs mrbc_init, mrbc_create_task(hello_bytecode), mrbc_run: it prints a greeting, waits using the scheduler, then returns. vm_tasks creates two tasks from first_bytecode.h and second_bytecode.h with a 48 KiB pool; both scripts call sleep_ms between prints, so the interleaved output shows two tasks sharing one scheduler and its wait states.

m5stack registers a display_write method on mrbc_class_object with mrbc_define_method: it accepts one String of up to 128 bytes, raises ArgumentError or TypeError otherwise, and returns the bytes written through M5Unified. It is build-tested only; no hardware behavior has been verified.
Each example is a standalone IDF project with its own CMakeLists.txt and main/idf_component.yml, shipped with generated bytecode headers so consumers build them without Ruby.

pages.title: How should applications use the scheduler and native bindings?
pages.purpose: Explain VM and pool ownership, task lifetimes, bounded waits, and the boundary between Ruby, native bindings, and peripheral interrupts.
pages.parent: How do I compile and run a Ruby script?

page_notes.content: The README's Application design section describes shared pool memory, per-task register and VM-slot costs, and the lifetime of trusted bytecode. Task.create makes a permanent task that can become dormant without closing its VM.

Use bounded scheduler waits in Ruby. In C, validate arity, type, and range before performing native work. Return after raising; distinguish borrowed arguments from transferred return values. Leave peripheral interrupts outside the VM and use notifications or queues to reach the VM task.

pages.title: What happens on pool exhaustion or an unhandled exception?
pages.purpose: Separate normal allocator and scheduler behavior from the two opt-in fatal policies.
pages.parent: Which Kconfig options control the VM?

page_notes.content: Kconfig disables pool statistics and profiling with ALLOC_LIBC. OOM_POOL_STATS prints total, used, and free pool bytes before invoking the usual ESP32 abort; it does not change the default OOM path.

PANIC_ON_UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION logs the exception and aborts at VM teardown. It does not change rescued exceptions, loader failures, or permanent tasks that skip teardown. ESP-IDF controls halt or reboot after an abort. tools/verify_idf.sh tests both default and opt-in behavior.

pages.title: How does CI build and emulate the component?
pages.purpose: The verification pipeline: test_app's sdkconfig profiles and compile-time contract assertions, verify_idf.sh's containerized builds and QEMU runs, the build.yml ESP-IDF version and chip matrix, and the lint and security workflows.

page_notes.content: test_app/main/main.c uses _Static_assert and #error pairs to verify every CONFIG_MRUBYC_* arrives as the identical compile definition, so consumer/VM contract drift fails compilation. It builds the real hello bytecode to smoke the runtime.

tools/verify_idf.sh runs inside the pinned espressif/idf container: the cache_safe profile must fail with the expected #error, test_app then builds for esp32/esp32c3/esp32s3/esp32c6 and seven sdkconfig.ci profiles, hello and vm_tasks build and run under QEMU on esp32/esp32c3 via tools/check_qemu.py, and m5stack gets a build-only check on esp32s3.

build.yml builds a matrix of ESP-IDF 5.5.6, 6.0.3, and 6.1.1 images pinned by sha256 digest, with ccache and tool caches keyed on sources and tools. workflow-lint.yml runs actionlint (with .github/actionlint.yaml registering ubuntu-26.04 labels) and ShellCheck; security.yml and scorecard.yml audit the workflows themselves.

pages.title: How does a release reach the ESP Component Registry?
pages.purpose: The tag-driven publish pipeline in upload.yml: packaging, staging upload via OIDC, a consumer build against the exact staged version, the production approval gate, attestation, production upload, and the GitHub release job.

page_notes.content: Tag mapping: manifest version 3.4.1 uses tag v3.4.1; a Registry revision like 3.4.1~1 replaces the tilde with a dot as v3.4.1.1. The manifest's version field always keeps the Registry form.

upload.yml packages the tagged commit once (tools/check_package.py verifies required files, exclusions, and the commit SHA recorded in the manifest), publishes that archive to the staging registry via OIDC, and builds the hello example against the exact staged version before requesting production approval.

The production job verifies the staged archive's SHA-256, attests build provenance, publishes via OIDC trusted uploaders, and a separate job then creates the GitHub release. Registry versions are immutable: re-run failed jobs rather than re-uploading, and bump the manifest revision plus tag only when the package itself changes.

One-time setup that CI cannot do itself: Registry Trusted Uploaders for OpenBlink/mrubyc-esp32 and upload.yml on both the staging and production registries, plus GitHub environments — required reviewers and release-tag restrictions belong on production only, while the separate staging environment only needs to allow release tags.

pages.title: How much flash and DRAM does the ESP32 example use?
pages.purpose: Use the README's measured ESP32 and ESP-IDF 6.1.1 comparison and explain what each reported size includes.

page_notes.content: README.md gives the reproducible idf.py size comparison against test_app/footprint, a C program with the same output as hello. The 32 KiB pool is already counted in static DRAM; do not add it twice. Do not generalize the numbers to other IDF versions, chips, configurations, or runtime memory usage.

pages.title: How do maintainers update bundled mruby/c?
pages.purpose: How maintainers pin an official release, update vendor/mrubyc, and verify the resulting tree in CI.
pages.parent: How does a release reach the ESP Component Registry?

page_notes.content: Maintainers update the release tag and SHA-256 pin in tools/import_upstream.py, which verifies the official release tarball before importing it.

Before touching vendor/, the import command compares MRUBY_VERSION and RITE_VERSION with the current tree. If they change or cannot be determined, follow the README's manual procedure and regenerate example bytecode with the matching mrbc.
Maintainers open and review the PR. The build workflow compares the vendored sources, ESP32 HAL, licenses, and component version with the pinned release.

pages.title: How do I build and verify changes locally?
pages.purpose: Developer workflow: building examples and test_app from a checkout with tools/build_app.sh, preparing packaged examples, smoke-testing the registry archive, and the repository's contribution conventions.

page_notes.content: tools/build_app.sh <example|test_app> <target> [profile] [reconfigure] builds inside an activated ESP-IDF environment, with BUILD_OUTPUT_DIR selecting the build directory. tools/generate_bytecode.sh regenerates the committed headers.

tools/prepare_example.py stages an example for Registry consumers, tools/check_qemu.py asserts expected console output under QEMU, tools/check_package.py validates an archive, and tools/smoke_registry.sh smoke-tests a built package.
Contribution rules from the README: use English, and for integration reports include the component version, ESP-IDF version, chip, and relevant configuration.
